lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you planned an information page. What does a caption do? (It says what a picture or a diagram shows.) Today: explain a complex idea so that anyone can follow it.
Start with an introduction that says what the reader will learn, and why it matters. Then give each part its own section, under a heading that tells the reader what is in it.
Organise by the idea's shape. A process goes in time order; causes and effects use “because” and “as a result”; a comparison uses “similarly” and “in contrast”; a problem leads to a solution.

Add graphics that teach: a labelled diagram for parts, a flowchart for a process, a table to compare. Use a graph for numbers and a map for places. Refer to each one (“Figure 1 shows…”) and give it a caption.
Choose precise words. Use the subject's own terms, like “evaporates” and “condenses”, not “goes up” and “turns back”. Define a hard term the first time: “Magma (melted rock underground) rises…”
Develop each section with facts, definitions, examples and quotations from experts. Join the ideas with transitions: “for example”, “as a result”, “in contrast”, “however”.
Keep a formal, calm tone. End with a conclusion that pulls the ideas together and says why they matter: “Volcanoes destroy, but they also build new land.”
Try it in the world: write a one-page guide to how something in your world works, with headings, one diagram with a caption and two defined words. Next: craft a narrative.

exercises.prompt: What should an explanation's introduction do?
choices: say what the reader will learn
exercises.hint: Think about what a reader needs before the details.
exercises.explain: An introduction tells the reader what they will learn and why it matters, so they can follow the rest.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of information to its graphic.
exercises.hint: Steps want arrows, parts want labels, amounts want bars and places want a map.
exercises.explain: A process suits a flowchart, parts a labelled diagram, numbers a bar chart, and places a map.

exercises.prompt: A heading tells the reader what a section is about.
exercises.hint: What is a heading for, on a page full of text?
exercises.explain: True: a clear heading lets the reader see what each section explains and find it again.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the most precise in this explanation? “Water vapour ___ into tiny drops in a cloud.”
exercises.hint: Which word would a scientist use?
exercises.explain: “Condenses” is the exact term for a gas turning into a liquid.

exercises.prompt: Sort the transitions by their job.
exercises.hint: Does each one move on in time, give a reason, or set two things side by side?
exercises.explain: “First” and “next” show time order; “as a result” and “because of this” show cause and effect; “in contrast” and “similarly” compare.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence defines a hard term for the reader?
choices: Lava, melted rock on the surface, cools fast.
Lava is a word that scientists use.
Lava is very hot and stuff.
exercises.hint: A definition says exactly what the word means.
exercises.explain: It says what lava is, melted rock on the surface, right where the word first appears.

exercises.prompt: Order the sections of an explanation of how a volcano erupts.
exercises.hint: Follow the process from start to finish, inside an introduction and a conclusion.
exercises.explain: The introduction, then magma forming, pressure building and the eruption, in time order, then the conclusion.

exercises.prompt: Which heading best fits a section about what makes magma rise?
exercises.hint: A good heading tells you exactly what the section explains.
exercises.explain: “Why magma rises” names the section's exact topic; the others are too vague to help a reader.

exercises.prompt: A figure should be mentioned in the text, not just placed on the page.
exercises.hint: How does the reader know when to look at it?
exercises.explain: True: “Figure 1 shows…” tells the reader when to look, and what to notice.

exercises.prompt: Match each structure to its signal words.
exercises.hint: Each structure has its own words for joining ideas.
exercises.explain: Time order: first, then, finally. Cause and effect: because, as a result. Compare: similarly, in contrast. Problem and solution: the issue, and one answer.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best caption for a diagram of the water cycle?
choices: Figure 2: water moves from sea to sky to land.
exercises.hint: A caption says what the graphic shows.
exercises.explain: It names the figure and says what it shows; the others tell the reader nothing.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is the most precise?
choices: The cables carry the deck's load to the towers.
The bridge has stuff that holds it up.
Things hold the bridge up somehow.
exercises.hint: Look for the sentence with exact names for the parts and what they do.
exercises.explain: It names the parts (cables, deck, towers) and says exactly what they do; the others are vague.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: formal and precise, or chatty and vague?
items: Magma rises because it is less dense.
Ash can travel hundreds of kilometres.
The vent carries magma to the surface.
It's basically a mountain that explodes.
exercises.hint: Look for exact terms and a calm tone, or slang and fuzzy words.
exercises.explain: The sentences about magma, the vent and the ash use exact terms in a calm tone; “like”, “loads of stuff” and “basically” are chatty and vague.

exercises.prompt: Order a paragraph that develops one idea.
items: Reason: it is less dense than rock.
Link: as a result, pressure builds.
Example: like a cork in water.
exercises.hint: Say the idea, give the reason, show an example, then link to what follows.
exercises.explain: A topic sentence, then the reason, then an example that makes it clear, then a link to the next idea.

exercises.prompt: You are explaining the heart to 8-year-olds. What should change?
choices: simpler words, with hard terms defined
exercises.hint: Think about who will read it.
exercises.explain: Younger readers need simpler words, and every hard term defined; a clear picture helps too.

exercises.prompt: A conclusion should add lots of new facts.
exercises.explain: False: it pulls the main ideas together and says why they matter; new facts belong in the sections.
